guide.title: Windsor, Connecticut: The State's First English Settlement
guide.intro: Windsor is Connecticut's first English settlement: a party of Plymouth Colony settlers under William Holmes arrived on September 26, 1633 to found a trading post, first called Dorchester after the Massachusetts town its second wave of settlers came from. The colony's General Court renamed it Windsor, after Windsor in Berkshire, England, on February 21, 1637. Palisado Green takes its name from a palisade hastily erected that year during the Pequot War, when settlers inside gave up their home lots to shelter families from outside it. Colonial Windsor ran a working river port in the West Indies trade, and tobacco has been grown here since 1640; the first shade-grown tobacco in the United States was raised on a half-acre plot in Windsor's Poquonock village in 1900, under cloth tents that mimicked Sumatran growing conditions. Oliver Ellsworth, a framer of the U.S. Constitution and the third Chief Justice of the United States, lived on Palisado Avenue.

sections.heading: A trading post that outlasted its palisade
sections.body: The Hooker and Chaffee mercantile firm kept a store and packing houses just off Palisado Green, shipping timber, wheat, livestock and tobacco to the West Indies and importing sugar, molasses, salt and British textiles and hardware; by the mid-1700s flaxseed had become one of the valley's most important exports. Shade tobacco reshaped the town's population in the 20th century: after World War I immigration restrictions cut the supply of European labor, growers recruited college students and workers from the American South, and beginning in 1947 Puerto Rican and Jamaican laborers came to Connecticut by the thousands, with many settling permanently in the area. Regional shade-tobacco acreage fell from about 30,000 acres in the 1930s to under 2,000 by 2006. The Luddy/Taylor Connecticut Valley Tobacco Museum, in Northwest Park, preserves that heritage in a restored curing shed.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body: Windsor sits just north of Hartford on I-91, and unusually for a Connecticut town of its size it has real passenger rail: CTrail Hartford Line and Amtrak Northeast Regional and Valley Flyer trains both stop at the 1870 depot at 41 Central Street in the middle of downtown, with 22 free parking spaces available 24/7. Connecticut Route 75 (Poquonock Avenue) runs north toward Bradley International Airport, which borders the town, and Route 159 (Palisado Avenue) is the historic spine past Palisado Green.

sections.heading: Where to eat and stay
sections.body: Bart's Drive-In on Palisado Avenue is a longtime local name for chili dogs, fried clams and soft serve — call ahead to confirm current hours. Tunxis Grill & Pizzeria, in a 100-year-old downtown building with brick booths, has served steaks, seafood and pizza since 2008. Yosi Kitchen on Hayden Station Road runs a Mediterranean and Middle Eastern kosher restaurant, market and bakery under one roof. For lodging, the Hartford/Windsor Marriott Airport on Day Hill Road runs a complimentary shuttle to Bradley International Airport, with the Hyatt House and a Residence Inn nearby.

faq.question: How do I get to Windsor?
faq.answer: By car via I-91, or by train — CTrail Hartford Line and Amtrak both stop at Windsor station, 41 Central Street, in the middle of downtown.

faq.question: Is there a train to Windsor?
faq.answer: Yes. Windsor station is a scheduled stop on the CTrail Hartford Line, with Amtrak Northeast Regional and Valley Flyer trains also serving it, and 22 free parking spaces.

faq.question: What is the Windsor Historical Society?
faq.answer: Founded in 1921, the society interprets nearly 400 years of Windsor history at 96 Palisado Avenue, with guided tours of two restored colonial houses — the 1758 Strong-Howard House and the 1767 Dr. Hezekiah Chaffee House. Call (860) 688-3813 to confirm current hours and admission before visiting.

faq.question: What is Oliver Ellsworth Homestead?
faq.answer: The home of Oliver Ellsworth, a framer of the U.S. Constitution and third Chief Justice of the United States, on Palisado Avenue. Run as a museum by the Connecticut Daughters of the American Revolution, open for tours May through the end of October.

faq.question: Is there a hotel in Windsor?
faq.answer: Yes — the Hartford/Windsor Marriott Airport, the Hyatt House Hartford North/Windsor and a Residence Inn by Marriott all cluster in the Day Hill Road corporate corridor, with shuttle service toward Bradley International Airport.

places.name: Windsor Historical Society
places.summary: Founded in 1921, the society interprets nearly 400 years of Windsor history through exhibition galleries, a research library and a museum shop; admission includes guided tours of the 1758 Strong-Howard House and the 1767 Dr. Hezekiah Chaffee House. Current hours and admission pricing are posted on the society's own site but could not be independently re-confirmed here — call (860) 688-3813 before visiting.

places.name: Luddy/Taylor Connecticut Valley Tobacco Museum
places.address: Northwest Park, 135 Lang Road, Windsor, CT 06095
places.summary: Run by the Connecticut Valley Tobacco Historical Society, preserving the heritage of the Connecticut River "Tobacco Valley" in a restored tobacco curing shed with historical and contemporary equipment. Free admission; self-guided visit runs 45-60 minutes. Season roughly first Thursday in March through last Saturday in October, open Friday and Saturday noon-4 p.m.

places.name: Northwest Park & Nature Center
places.summary: A 473-acre town-owned park with 12 miles of hiking trails, grown back from former tobacco farmland into forest and field habitat. Free and open dawn to dusk; a working maple sugar house, farm animals and year-round programming including a coffee house concert series and annual country fair. Nature center open Mon-Sat 8:30 a.m.-4:30 p.m., Sun 1-4 p.m.

places.name: Oliver Ellsworth Homestead
places.address: 788 Palisado Avenue, Windsor, CT 06095 (the National Register listing gives 778 Palisado Avenue; the two sources disagree by one house number)
places.summary: The home of Oliver Ellsworth, a delegate to the Continental Congress and third Chief Justice of the U.S. Supreme Court; both George Washington and John Adams visited. David Ellsworth built the original structure in 1740, and Oliver Ellsworth's family moved into a new house in 1782. The Ellsworth family transferred it to the Connecticut Daughters of the American Revolution in 1903, which has operated it as a house museum since. Open for tours May through the end of October.

places.name: Windsor Art Center
places.summary: Founded in 2007 in a restored freight house near Windsor station, a 1,500-square-foot gallery presenting rotating visual art exhibitions plus musical performances, artist talks and workshops. Exhibition hours Thu 6-8 p.m., Sat 10 a.m.-4 p.m., Sun 11 a.m.-4 p.m.; free on-site parking. Also runs adult and kids' art classes and Sunday evening yoga.

places.name: Tunxis Grill & Pizzeria
places.summary: Established in 2008 in a 100-year-old downtown building with brick booths and an open kitchen, serving steaks, seafood, pasta, pizza, salads and burgers for lunch and dinner seven days a week. Hours Sun-Wed 11 a.m.-9 p.m., Thu-Sat to 10 p.m. Phone (860) 688-6429.

places.name: Yosi Kitchen
places.summary: A Mediterranean and Middle Eastern kosher restaurant, market and caterer under one roof, with shawarma, falafel, schnitzel and fresh-baked pita. Open year-round: Mon-Thu 9 a.m.-5 p.m., Fri 9 a.m.-3 p.m., Sun 11 a.m.-4 p.m., closed Saturdays. Phone (860) 688-6677.
